paragraphs.text: Chapter 5. Light

Of all the science I’ve studied over the years—as a research neuroscientist, in my role hosting many of the world’s most qualified doctors and scientists on my podcast, and in my own real-world experience—light, and the incredible influence it has on every aspect of our health, is the subject that has thrilled and surprised me the most.

As a master’s student I worked on the visual pathways that control circadian rhythms, and in graduate school and during my postdoc fellowship, and in my own lab, I researched visual circuits that convert light energy—photons, that is—into conscious visual perception, or what is commonly referred to as eyesight. My lab also spent a few years exploring the connections between our eyes and the cerebellum. Turns out, our eyes and our cerebellum—or “mini brain”—are in an ongoing dialogue that helps us orient in space. We will get back to the cerebellum later when we discuss learning in chapter 6.

But as my lab explored the visual system, papers kept coming out showing how light either supports or damages the health of our cells. In some cases these findings were about how light affects the skin. In other cases, it was about how light impacts our health via our eyes in ways that are separate from eyesight. Given that so much of my training centered around our visual system, that research intrigued me. Not just because it was in my wheelhouse but also because of how actionable it was. It could be applied easily to daily life, and impact health in potent ways. So I voraciously read every one of those studies. I also knew one of the pioneers in this field. Glen Jeffery, PhD, at the University College London, a former colleague of mine from the field of visual system development, began to study how particular types and sources of light either help or hurt human physiology. His lab also studied how light affected longevity. [^1] I connected with him periodically to get a sense of what was on the horizon. While his is not the only lab working on the relationship between light and health, Glen is a leader in the formal study of this topic. We have him to thank for taking what were largely anecdotal observations put forth by niche online communities and testing them in controlled studies including clinical trials.

Over those years, I was also spending more and more time indoors, under LED lights—both during the day and at night. Such is life in a lab. My colleagues all did the same. So did my friends in medicine, tech, design, and, once smartphones hit the world full force in 2010, pretty much everyone else. I, and some of my more health-conscious colleagues, started to wonder if all that time indoors under the LED lights was part of the reason a lot of us were feeling so lousy.

Now we know that it almost certainly was. The lack of full-spectrum sunlight, and the use of LED light was no doubt directly damaging our bodies, inside and out, by impairing cellular health. Now of course, I can’t be sure it was all due to indoor lighting, but at one point my hair started falling out, I was always tired in the afternoon, and my joints ached. And I was exercising and eating well at the time, and my life was no more stressful than it is now.

Eventually I decided to use light as a tool, not just to get my sleep right but to improve other aspects of my health. I was amazed by what happened. My hair grew back—like crazy, in fact. I got far fewer colds and other respiratory infections. My mood even lifted. Mind you, I was in my forties then, and I’m in my fifties now, and still with the addition of a few simple protocols, my general health improved markedly. There are different levers of health but based on the data from Glen’s lab and others, I treat my relationship to sunlight and indoor lighting as key levers for health.

My experience is anecdotal, but we now have evidence to support why and precisely how the use of light can improve cellular, organ, and body-wide health. It is an area of health just as crucial as sleep, exercise, or nutrition. Moreover, we now know the best ways to capture the benefits of different types of light. Which is why it deserves its own chapter here.

While light as a tool for health is not discussed as often as it should be, it is not new, and its origins are definitely not fringe; we’ve long known that there was a connection between sunlight and well-being. And in many regions of the world, hospitals still take patients outside for the age-old practice of sunlight exposure to promote recovery from certain ailments. [^2] And photobiomodulation has been studied and used by serious scientists and physicians since the early 1900s. [^3] The Danish physician Niels Finsen was actually awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1903 for his discovery that light can be used to treat various diseases including tuberculosis of the skin, or lupus.

Nowadays, photobiomodulation has been shown to be effective for treating acne, [^4] accelerating wound healing, [^5] and promoting hair growth, [^6] as well as reducing pain [^7] and even improving blood sugar regulation. [^8] Studies have also demonstrated the efficacy of photobiomodulation for offsetting age-related vision loss [^9] and for improving hormone health. [^10] That’s not all; light has also been shown to improve heart [^11] and GI tract health [^12] and to help combat various autoimmune conditions. [^13]

And of course, there are countless positive effects of viewing sunlight on your circadian rhythm. As you recall from chapter 1, viewing low solar angle sunlight in the morning and again in the afternoon sets your sleep-wake cycle correctly, increases your daytime mood, alertness and focus, and immune system function, and promotes better sleep at night. It is not exaggerating to say that light is medicine, especially sunlight.

And like any medicine, the effects of light depend on the type, intensity, duration, and timing of its delivery. For example, whereas sunlight in the morning and daytime is beneficial, viewing bright lights (especially from LED sources) too close to your bedtime spikes your cortisol levels, quashes your melatonin, and disrupts your blood sugar regulation (as discussed in Sleep Protocol 3). That affects your sleep that night and your energy the next morning. And certain wavelengths of light—in particular those emitted by most LED sources—may also accelerate cellular aging and promote disease progression by damaging cells in the retina, cornea, and brain, according to studies in animal models. [^14]

While all these effects of light might sound tricky to navigate, it’s actually quite simple. You just need to know which types of light are beneficial to view, which are detrimental, and how and when to maximize one and minimize the other. In this chapter, I’ll teach you.
What Is Light?
First we need to discuss what light is, exactly.

Obviously, light makes things visible. Any light source, be it the sun, a lamp, a candle flame, or the glow from a phone screen makes things visible because it emits energy. Light sources vary by type and amount of energy; that’s what makes them different from one another.

Recall from chapter 1 that light is comprised of a broad range of wavelengths, from very short wavelengths to very long ones. Some of these wavelengths are visible to humans—they make up what we call the visible spectrum of red, green, blue, and so on. Other wavelengths of light, such as ultraviolet and infrared, are invisible to us.

Short wavelengths of light are, as their name suggests, waves of energy where the peaks and the troughs of the wave are very close together. Long wavelengths of light are the opposite; the peaks and troughs of long wavelength light are relatively far apart.

The sun emits an extremely broad range of short, medium, and long wavelengths. The entire visible spectrum is held inside sunlight. That’s why sunlight through a prism comes through as a rainbow on the other side. The prism slows down and bends the light, and each wavelength exits at a different angle, spreading the light into the full visible spectrum of red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo, and violet.

Green, blue, and purple light are shorter in wavelength compared to yellow, orange, and red light, which are longer. Sunlight (in the absence of a prism) appears white or pale yellow. The sky turns colorful at dawn and dusk because, as you may recall from chapter 1, when the sun is low in the sky, components of the atmosphere reduce the amount of shorter wavelengths reaching our eyes—a process called Rayleigh scattering—leaving us primarily seeing the longer wavelengths of red, orange, and yellow. The sun of course always emits the same wavelengths of energy regardless of where it happens to be in the sky. Which visible wavelengths arrive at our eyes is what determines how the sun appears to us, and the effect it will have on us.

Then there are the invisible wavelengths. Sunlight includes wavelengths shorter than blue or violet that are (unimaginatively) called ultraviolet (UV) light. We can’t perceive UV light but it’s there, radiating down on us all day. (Though interesting to note that bees can see UV, and squirrels can see it too, possibly to help them detect predators at night. Some species of flying squirrels actually have UV fluorescence that causes their bellies to glow a bubblegum pink.) [^15] The sun also emits wavelengths longer than red light, appropriately called infrared (IR) light. We humans can’t see IR, but we can feel it as warmth. Though we have engineered technologies to see IR emissions—that’s what night vision goggles do.

The sun also emits small amounts of X-ray energy, which is made up of very short wavelength radiation, even shorter than UV. And, like with UV and IR, we can’t see X-rays, but they are there. X-rays pass through our skin but are absorbed by our bones, teeth, and other dense tissues. That’s how X-ray machines work: They are designed to send out concentrated X-rays so their patterns of absorption can be captured on film or by a digital sensor, allowing your doctor or dentist to see different structures inside your body that absorb those X-rays to varying degrees.

Whether visible or invisible, these wavelengths travel in a similar pattern—not as a line but, well, as a wave, moving up and down, up and down. Shorter wavelengths of light go through many more up-down-up-down cycles as they travel from one point to another; longer wavelengths go through fewer. Thus, we often refer to short wavelengths of light as high frequency light and long wavelengths of light as low frequency.

Mentions of UV light can trigger concerns, so let me address that now. Whether light exposure is harmful, beneficial, or benign depends on the type, intensity, duration, and timing. All light energy is radiation. Often when people hear the word radiation they think radioactive. The radiation from visible light is not harmful because it doesn’t have enough energy to perturb the atoms in our body. But here’s where type, duration, and the other factors matter. Some forms of non-ionizing light radiation can disrupt our cells if we are exposed to too much of it. For example, we need some UV light exposure each day. But excessive exposure can cause genetic mutations in our cells by causing the formation of abnormal bonds in our DNA. [^16]

Wavelength and intensity of light are inversely related to one another. Put in practical terms, you can be exposed to a lot of long wavelength light, like red or IR light, without damaging your skin. It takes comparatively less exposure to short wavelength UV light to cause a sunburn. But that doesn’t mean short wavelength, high frequency light is inherently bad for us. Again, we come back to this core idea: Dosage matters. We all need some UV light from the sun to reach our skin, where it sets off a cascade of reactions that results in the production of vitamin D, which is critical for calcium absorption, bone health, immune health, and more. [^17] But too much UV exposure can lead to a sunburn, as I mentioned above, and cause premature aging of your skin, as well as DNA mutations that lead to certain skin cancers. [^18] And because long wavelength IR is so low energy (remember, wavelength and intensity are inversely related), we need relatively long sun exposure times to enjoy its benefits. The challenge is getting enough IR and NIR (infrared and near-infrared) light from the sun without also getting excessive UV exposure, but it can be done. There’s a protocol for it.

I’m aware that none of what I’ve shared with you thus far tells you exactly how light can change your cells. As wavelengths travel through space, in that up-and-down cycle, they hit various surfaces, big and small: a mountain range, a tree, this page, your hand. These surfaces absorb or reflect wavelengths. But sometimes they pass right through. Light can pass right through your body, for example, and as it does it can change the molecular properties of the cells it encounters and the components within them, such as in the example of excessive UV-altering DNA structure of, say, skin cells. Here are two more examples, this time with light playing positive roles in cellular function: Studies suggest that red, NIR, and IR light can enhance the functioning of your mitochondria, the energy producing organelles in your cells. [^19] Data suggest that NIR and IR may also trigger the release of a gas called nitric oxide that acts on your vascular and lymphatic cells and causes them to dilate, allowing for more lymph fluid and blood to move through them. [^20]

There are more examples in the protocols that follow. You’ll learn how to use light—in some cases sunlight, and in other cases artificial light of specific wavelengths—to improve your physical and mental health. Also here are recommendations for in-home lighting and light devices that emit or block specific wavelengths of light, which you can use to achieve specific benefits, such as increased morning and daytime energy levels, better glucose regulation, and even better eyesight. In chapter 1, we explored how light helps with sleep; now it’s time to see its immediate effects on other important aspects of our health.

As you read these protocols, remember this: While it might seem fantastical that light can do so many positive things for our brain and body, it actually makes perfect sense. Light is energy that the cells in our body can absorb and use. The very first law of thermodynamics is that energy can’t be destroyed or created de novo; it can only be converted from one form to another. So let’s discuss the ways you can convert light energy into cellular energy, which leads to improvements in physical energy, vision, skin, mood, and heart health… and more.
I hope this powerful lever will no longer be overlooked.

Note: If you are reading this book from beginning to end, you’ll realize as you encounter Light Protocols 1, 2, and 3 that these are essentially the same as protocols covered in chapter 1 and chapter 3. You may be thinking, “Does he have a memory issue, or think I have one?” The answer is: no and no.

The practices I suggest in this chapter are indeed found in earlier ones. But, because many people may read this book out of order, I wanted to be sure that these crucial protocols would not be missed. Moreover, the information that follows is not a carbon copy of the protocols in chapter 1 or chapter 3. I include new information about the mechanisms behind the “critical window” in the first hour after you wake up, whereby your SCN can amplify your morning cortisol levels… if and only if you give it the right stimulus. I also cover new information about viewing light at specific times to adjust your cortisol rhythm, so you can avoid what is commonly referred to as “burnout,” but is often a mistiming in your daily cortisol peak. I also include more options for indoor lighting—some were mentioned only briefly in previous chapters; others are new. All that said, if you feel you are already versed enough in these first three protocols and most importantly, you are already doing them on a daily basis, feel free to skip to Light Protocol 4.
LIGHT PROTOCOL 1 View Bright Light in the First Hour After Waking to (Further) Increase Your Morning Cortisol Levels
WHAT TO DO

• Get morning sunlight in your eyes as soon as possible after waking. If the sun hasn’t risen yet, or is otherwise inaccessible, view a 10,000 lux artificial light. Either one will significantly elevate your post-waking morning cortisol levels, which is highly beneficial if it occurs in the first hour of your day.

• The timing will vary based on when you wake up, and where you live. Refer to the information below to figure out what’s best for you. Ten to thirty minutes is a good general rule, but even if you can only grab five, do it. Some is better than none.
HOW IT WORKS

It is hard to overstate the positive impact of this protocol on your energy, mood, focus, stress levels, immune system, and, of course, sleep. If you’ve read chapter 1, you might be thinking: Does this protocol sound familiar? Yes, I’m recommending a similar behavioral tool here, but emphasizing different benefits. Stay with me.
I can hear all the questions running through your head, so for this protocol, let’s tackle these first.

You’re probably thinking, “Wait—I have to get up and watch the sunrise every day?” No. You don’t. If you wake up early enough, and the sky is clear, great! Do that. But most people can’t. And you don’t need to. The key thing here is to view bright light in the first hour after waking. This applies even if your normal wake-up time is noon.

“What if I wake up before the sun is out?” Another question I hear often. Again, not a problem. That is where a 10,000 lux artificial light can really help. It’s not a replacement for sunlight, but if you wake up before sunrise, I suggest getting one of these lights and looking at it for ten minutes or so upon waking. Then, if you can, get outside for some early natural light once the sun has risen. If you’re off to work at an office before sunrise, these lights are a game changer.

“I can’t see the sun where I live, so what should I do?” I have good news for you. You need to get sunlight in your eyes, but you do not need to see the sun. Some days it’s clear, and other days it’s overcast. Sunlight still comes through on cloudy days. Maybe you’re thinking: “Not where I live!” Really? Consider how bright it is at 8:00 a.m. on a densely clouded winter day in Seattle, which is the northernmost major city in the contiguous US. Then consider what it’s like at midnight the night before. Unless you live at one of the earth’s poles in winter—which I’m guessing you don’t—there is always some sunlight during the daytime. So view it within an hour of waking. Let’s keep going with those common questions.

“Can I wear sunglasses?” It’s best to view morning sunlight without them. Wearing corrective lenses such as eyeglasses or contact lenses is fine, even if they include UV protection. Don’t wear a brimmed hat, however. The neurons in your eyes that you need to stimulate here respond to light coming from above and in front of your eyes, and a brimmed hat will block it.

“Can I blink?” Yes! Never force yourself to stare at sunlight, or any bright light for that matter. It can damage your eyes to do so. People vary in their sensitivity to light, so if this is hard for you, squint and look to the area adjacent to the sun as needed. This shouldn’t hurt.

“Can I get my morning sunlight through a window?” While better than nothing, the glass used for most windows filters out too much of the wavelengths of light you need. Thus, go outside. Bring your morning coffee, tea, or a glass of water. Bring your dog, kids, partner, or a friend along with you if you like. Yes, your dog will benefit too. After all, the same circuits and mechanisms that underlie this protocol are present in humans and dogs (and horses, goats, and squirrels, as I’ve mentioned, and all diurnal mammals). And of course you can walk, jog, skip rope, or do calisthenics as you view bright light too. If you take an hour walk, or schedule a run or a yoga session outside, even better, as sunlight and exercise can synergize to increase your early morning cortisol levels. Whatever you do, just don’t spend the whole time looking down at your phone. That will negate the effect you’re seeking.

“How long should I view morning sunlight to get the maximum effect?” As I mentioned, the answer depends on sunlight availability but a good general rule of thumb is this: On clear mornings shoot for a minimum of ten minutes, on partially cloudy days, get a minimum of twenty minutes, and on very overcast days, thirty minutes. If you view a 10,000 lux artificial light beforehand, for any of the reasons discussed already, you’ll need less time viewing sunlight—about half as much—to get the same effect.
It’s hard to be more specific than this because sunlight availability is shaped by the time of day, time of year, weather, and location.

And, once more: “What if I wake up before sunrise, then what?” This is by far the most common question I hear. Unless you have powers that I am not aware of, you will have to wait for the sun to come out to see sunlight. Get your in-the-first-hour-of-waking bright light by viewing a 10,000 lux artificial light. Ten thousand lux artificial light devices are not as good as sunlight, because they don’t contain the same array and balance of wavelengths present in sunlight as discussed in the introduction to this chapter. But they will elevate your morning cortisol levels, which is your goal in this protocol. [^21] They cost about $100 to $150. Some are portable and suitable for travel. And, again, if you rely on a 10,000 lux light first thing in the morning, you’ll still want to get five to twenty minutes or so of natural sunlight exposure to your eyes once the sun comes out. Most people find that having a 10,000 lux light in their bathroom or kitchen works well for their morning routines.

If you do use a 10,000 lux light, you needn’t be obsessed with the viewing distance, nor do you have to worry about intermittently stepping or pivoting away from the light while preparing for your day. Just aim to be in front of it at a distance of about one to two feet for at least ten minutes total in the first hour after waking. More is fine, but again people vary in their sensitivity to light and some find that after ten minutes of 10,000 lux light they feel too awake! Other people can handle more exposure.

And if you have a question about my schedule: Because I typically wake up before the sun is out, I have a 10,000 lux light in my bathroom and my kitchen. I turn them on within a few minutes of waking and leave them on as I brush my teeth and prepare for my day. Once the sun is up, I go outside and view sunlight. That way, on days when I need to commute to work early or exercise before the sun is up, I know I have already spiked my morning cortisol. And when I travel, I bring a small portable 10,000 lux unit and use it in the same way. It’s a fantastic tool but it’s not a replacement for sunlight.

“Does viewing my computer screen or phone work to replace morning sunlight or 10,000 lux light?” Alas, no. Your phone screen is far too dim and far too narrow a spectrum to accomplish the effect here. Diabolically, however, your phone or computer screen is plenty bright enough to stimulate cortisol release if it’s viewed at night. And that is bad. And your phone or computer is plenty bright enough to suppress your melatonin levels. Also bad!

By now you may be asking (or shouting): “Wait, why in the world would I want to increase my cortisol levels? Isn’t cortisol a stress hormone? Isn’t that a bad thing?” Okay, maybe if you read this book in order, you already know the answer, but I’ll repeat it here: Most people think cortisol is a stress hormone to avoid, but you absolutely want to have high cortisol levels in the first hours of your day. The science shows us why.
The Natural Cortisol Cycle

Sleep Protocol 1 explains the science behind how viewing morning sunlight impacts your circadian rhythm. As a brief reminder: When you view sunlight, or a 10,000 lux light, it activates cells in your eyes that convert light into electrical signals. Those signals are relayed to the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), your master circadian clock, located above the roof of your mouth in your hypothalamus. The SCN in turn releases chemical and electrical signals that coordinate the activities of the trillions of twenty-four-hour clocks found in every cell and organ of your body into a coherent set of rhythms. The physiological and psychological benefits that circadian coordination brings about are many.

But the SCN is not a one-trick pony. It serves another crucial role that is seldom discussed but, frankly, just as important. Your SCN can also stimulate a significant increase in your cortisol levels in the first sixty minutes after you wake up. It’s time restricted, meaning it can only occur in this short window. If you miss it, it’s gone—at least until the next day.

This is not a window you want to miss! Because whereas surges in cortisol are generally not advantageous if they occur in the afternoon, the evening, or at night, as I’ve mentioned, you actually want your cortisol levels to be very high in the first hours of your day.

Cortisol has gotten a bad rap. It’s been labeled the stress hormone and indeed, this hormone made in your adrenal glands is released during times of stress. But cortisol is also released when you wake up each morning. More accurately, you wake up each morning because cortisol is released. You read that right. Cortisol is the hormone that ensures you have the energy to get out of bed and lean into your daily activities. That is because cortisol’s fundamental role is to cause the release of stored fuels in your liver and muscles, which shifts the state of your brain and body from sleep to one of physical and mental readiness. The technical term for this process, which you might remember from chapter 3, is called the cortisol awakening response (CAR). Cortisol is not just a stress hormone. It’s an energy-releasing hormone. (See Stress Control Protocol 5 if you’d like a reminder.)

When we view cortisol in this way, we start to understand that it’s not something to be avoided at all. Rather, it is something to harness and use to our advantage. Our body has designated pathways and mechanisms to do just that. It allows for what’s called the healthy twenty-four-hour cortisol curve, which follows the pattern below:
• 1 Very low in the 1 to 2 hours prior to bedtime
• 2 At its absolute lowest in the first half of your night’s sleep
• 3 Rising slowly in the second half of your night’s sleep
• 4 Rising sharply in the 30 minutes prior to your desired wake-up time
• 5 Rising sharply even more in the first 1 to 2 hours after you wake up
• 6 Peaking about 30 minutes to 3 hours after waking
• 7 Gradually decreasing across the early and late afternoon
• 8 Repeat…

Countless studies now show that allowing this natural cycle to operate without disruption helps optimize our sleep, cognition, and energy levels as well as mood and immune system function. [^22] By contrast, altering this cycle such that evening or nighttime cortisol levels are too high (or morning cortisol levels are too low) can lead to problems in all these areas. Studies of night shift workers have been crucial in uncovering these connections. [^23] A chronic disruption to the ideal cycle is referred to as a flattening of the cortisol curve. This flattening causes anxiety, sleep disturbances, low daytime energy, and mood disruptions as well as impaired immune resistance to viral, bacterial, and other infections. [^24]
Cortisol and Stress

Keep in mind that just because we are framing cortisol as not purely a stress hormone does not mean it is not related to stress. It is. Stress triggers the release of cortisol. [^25] If you experience stress at any point during the day or night, you can and should expect a spike in your cortisol to occur. That’s perfectly normal, healthy, and adaptive—because that spike will provide you with the immediate physical and mental energy you need to deal with whatever stressor you might face. [^26] Stress-triggered cortisol levels typically return to baseline within about one hour or so. In fact, you can experience a lot of cortisol spikes above baseline per day (or night) before it ever becomes problematic for your health. I’m not suggesting you seek out stress, but as we discussed in chapter 3, humans evolved to deal with it in a variety of forms. Raising kids, traffic, difficult people, the pressures of work, school, or athletics, the state of the world… many of these are indeed stressful at times, and cortisol makes sure you have the fuel to deal with each one.

Cortisol spikes that occur shortly before sleep are where problems begin. That increase is often what prevents people from falling asleep, and what causes the classic stress-induced sleep disturbance of waking up at 3:00 a.m. and not falling back asleep. One night of that happening, no biggie. Two nights in a row? Hard, but manageable. However, three or more nights of stress-induced sleep disturbances really start to take a toll on your mental and physical health.
Cortisol and Light

And now we get back to the protocol suggested here. I discussed how to deal with both acute and chronic stress in chapter 3. What we didn’t discuss is that when you get your twenty-four-hour cortisol curve correct, it makes both kinds of stress much easier to deal with. And to get your twenty-four-hour cortisol curve correct we need to… view morning sunlight (or 10,000 lux light) in the first hour after waking. It not only boosts your morning cortisol levels, but also helps ensure your nighttime cortisol is kept low. This has immediate benefits you can feel within minutes and that last all day, among them improved mood, focus, and energy. Think of it as the optimal start signal for your day. Because from the perspective of your brain and body, that’s exactly what it is.

Here are the basics of how it works, plus some additional information pertinent to the twenty-four-hour cortisol cycle. Your cortisol level at any one moment, and your overall twenty-four-hour cortisol cycle, are controlled via the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis, which we discussed in chapter 3. Neurons in an area of your hypothalamus called the PVN (paraventricular nucleus) extend wirelike projections into your pituitary, a gland that resembles two small marbles in a sock hanging out the base of your brain. [^27] One of those marbles sits in front of the other, and this is called the anterior pituitary. Your PVN neurons release corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH) to cause your anterior pituitary cells to release adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH) into your bloodstream. Next, the ACTH travels to your adrenal glands and stimulates the release of cortisol into your bloodstream. Voila! Cortisol then causes energy to be released from various organs and cells in your body. Cortisol does many other things, but one more that’s relevant here: Unlike adrenaline, which is also released from your adrenal glands and increases your energy level, cortisol can cross the blood-brain barrier. That means it has action on the body, such as mobilizing glucose for fuel, but also can increase the excitability of the neurons in your brain involved in alertness, focus, memory formation, and even motivation.

The PVN also detects when cortisol levels in your blood get high. It then reduces its release of CRH, which in turn reduces ACTH release, which results in less cortisol release. This is called a negative feedback loop; when the level of cortisol reaching the brain is very high, less cortisol is triggered to be released. In that way, it is like how many home thermostats work. For example, if the temperature in a room becomes too high from the level you’ve set, the thermostat shuts the heat off.

This self-regulation process takes a bit of time to take effect, which is why a short-term spike in cortisol is no big deal. An hour or so afterward, you’re back to your baseline level, appropriate for that time of day. But with frequent spikes, you start to alter your normal twenty-four-hour cortisol cycle. Cortisol surges at 9:00 p.m. for a few nights in a row and the next thing you know, your next-morning levels are lower than they should be and your PVN is then primed to release more cortisol later that night.

There is a name for this domino effect. It’s called chronic-stress-induced burnout. Alas, for many, this is the norm, especially now that a good number of people lie in bed looking at their phone in the first and last hour of each day, which, for reasons you’ll soon understand, sets them up for lower-than-needed cortisol levels in the morning and greater-than-desired cortisol levels at night.

So in a way, a better name for chronic-stress-induced burnout would be “wrongly-timed-cortisol-induced-burnout,” because, again, you want your morning cortisol high. I already listed some of the immediate benefits of stimulating cortisol in the hour after waking, but perhaps by now you can also identify another: If you do, you not only get enormous benefits in energy, focus, and mood right away, you also kickstart that crucial negative feedback loop that ensures that your levels of cortisol will be dropping as you head into the afternoon and evening. Your cortisol levels will be very low as you progress into sleep.

That’s how all the pieces come together: In that special window in the first hour after you wake up, when your SCN can also stimulate a significant increase in your cortisol levels, you can bypass the negative feedback loop and stimulate the release of more cortisol even though its levels are already high. In fact, your SCN does so both through the HPA pathway and via a separate, parallel pathway involving direct activation of your sympathetic nervous system. [^28] We can refer to that second pathway as the MLIC pathway (for morning-light-induced-cortisol pathway). And, as the name indicates, the way to activate the MLIC pathway is by viewing bright light.

As a final note, researchers have studied the use of bright artificial light in the first hour of the day not just for this, but as a therapeutic intervention for seasonal affective disorder (SAD), a diagnosable mood disorder characterized by depression that fluctuates with the seasons, worsening in the colder, darker months. [^29] Rates of this condition are particularly high among people who have major depression or bipolar disorder. In one study, people diagnosed with seasonal affective disorder were treated with twenty, forty, or sixty minutes of 10,000 lux light in the morning. [^30] Even the shortest exposure was sufficient to relieve depression among the participants, according to a self-reported questionnaire. Other studies have shown similar results. [^31] Newer studies have shown that reducing the amount of bright light reaching your eyes in the final one to two hours of your day leads to improvements in mood and sleep, and to various mental and physical performance benefits as well. [^32]

In the last ten years, it’s become clear that far more people are suffering from SAD or SAD-like symptoms due to device usage in the early and late hours of the day. In chapter 1, we discussed the severe negative effects of shift work on long-term health, and the fact that nowadays most adults and kids—most (!)—qualify as shift workers due to this kind of device usage. How can that be? Well, remember—even the brightest device screens are too dim to trigger meaningful cortisol increases in the first hour of your day, and even the dimmest screens are more than bright enough to trigger cortisol increases at night. That is, unless you filter out the short wavelengths reaching your eyes—which we talk about in the next protocol.
COMMON QUESTIONS
Does it matter if this light hits my skin or are the eyes all that count here
This protocol is concerned with viewing light only. Later protocols in this chapter will address the need for sunlight on skin and how to balance that exposure with cautions about sun damage.
LIGHT PROTOCOL 2 View Sunlight in the Late Afternoon and/or Early Evening to Help Buffer Against Negative Effects of Artificial Light at Night
WHAT TO DO

• View sunlight in the afternoon and early evening, for five to thirty minutes. Follow the same general guidelines as for Light Protocol 1. Simply go outside, take off your sunglasses (eyeglasses and contacts are fine), and face in the direction of the setting sun. Don’t wear a brimmed hat. And again, don’t stare at the sun; blink as needed.
• Do not replace late afternoon/evening sunlight viewing with a 10,000 lux artificial light. It’s too bright, and the wavelengths these devices emit can mess up your sleep-wake cycle.
HOW IT WORKS

As discussed in Sleep Protocol 2, melatonin, which facilitates falling and staying asleep, begins to increase in the late afternoon and early evening and sharply rises in the hour before your natural bedtime (which, by the way, tends to arrive about fifteen to sixteen hours after your morning sunlight viewing). It continues to rise into the night, before gradually decreasing as morning approaches. Melatonin levels are lowest in the morning and highest at night. In other words, when cortisol is high, melatonin is low, and when cortisol is low, melatonin is high. [^33]

Bright light robustly suppresses melatonin, and it causes the release of cortisol as explained in chapter 3. [^34] Blue lights, screen lights, and LEDs, all of which emit lots of short wavelengths, are especially potent at suppressing melatonin. Bright LEDs, commonly used in bathrooms, bedrooms, and hallways, are short-wavelength enriched. It takes less than thirty seconds of bright LED exposure to the eyes to significantly reduce your melatonin levels. So if you pick up your phone at night, or flip on the lights… you’re exposing yourself to the kind of light that will suppress melatonin. Late afternoon and early evening sunlight viewing helps mitigate these negative effects.

Why do I suggest you not use a 10,000 lux artificial light as a replacement for evening sunlight, when I already suggested it as a replacement for morning sunlight in the previous protocol? The reason has to do with wavelengths, discussed earlier in this chapter. Low solar angle sunlight is lower in UV and the short visible wavelengths, which is why sunrises and sunsets often appear orange, pink, or even deep red. Those longer wavelengths help inform your brain that night is coming, and it should prepare for sleep. Too much short wavelength light—especially if it’s bright, and 10,000 lux is bright—will alter your sleep-wake cycle.

You’ll notice, just as in the previous protocol, that I’m not suggesting specific times to view late afternoon or early evening sunlight. Again, that is because schedules vary from person to person, and the time of day when the sun sets varies according to your location and the time of year. Luckily, you can get the desired effect without being overly precise about the timing. Just aim to view sunlight at some point after the sun is directly overhead and before it sets.

This doesn’t mean that you should avoid sunlight or artificial light during other parts of the day. Researchers from Rush University ran a small study where, for one week, people experienced bright light exposure for up to five hours by combining outdoor exposure to sunlight and indoor exposure to 10,000 lux light during the day. [^35] They called it “the bright week.” The following week, the light exposure was dimmer; people spent two and a half hours outdoors at most, and wore light-obscuring goggles when they did. That was “the dim week.” The researchers found that light-induced melatonin suppression at night was greater during the dim week than during the bright week (though some participants showed greater differences than others). Bright light exposure during the day partially prevented light-induced melatonin suppression at night.

Seems paradoxical, given that light suppresses melatonin, right? Yes, until we look at another mechanism at work here. Another small study from the Netherlands measured melatonin levels, body temperature, and skin blood flow (all markers of circadian rhythmicity) of twelve women and noted how sleepy they reported feeling, according to when they viewed light in the evening and at night. [^36] They divided subjects into three groups. One group viewed dim light at night. Another group also viewed dim light at night but also viewed bright lights beforehand, late in the evening. The third group viewed bright light in the early evening, and then dim lights at night. All three groups saw some reduction in melatonin, which is not surprising given that light viewing suppresses melatonin production any time of day or night. But the third group—the group that saw early evening bright light plus late-night dim light—had a less dramatic melatonin drop. This again supports the idea that early evening light exposure can partially inoculate us against the negative effects of bright light at night.

These studies may be small, but they point to the importance of viewing sunlight in the late afternoon and early evening, and avoiding bright light exposure at night. It’s worth noting that it may be especially important for adolescents to avoid bright light at night, as one study showed that early evening sunlight exposure did not protect them against the melatonin-reducing effects of bright light as it did for adults. [^37] This may also mean that adolescents are particularly sensitive to the negative effects of bright artificial lights and screens at night.

The reasons to try to offset the negative effects of bright light at night are not just related to sleep. Animal studies have shown that bright light exposure to the eyes late at night activates pro-depression circuitries. [^38] And as we’ve already covered, human studies have shown strong links between nighttime bright light exposure, cortisol increases, melatonin suppression, and mood disturbances. If you or your child happens to view bright light in the hours before sleep now and again, perhaps from a movie or a night out, that’s no cause for concern. If you make a habit of keeping bright artificial lights on late at night, however, and you notice your moods are shifting for the worse, that could be why.

As you’re probably realizing, modern life—with all its lighting options and screens everywhere—is not oriented around daylight fluctuations in the way it once was. Humans used to wake up and go to sleep with the sun. We had no choice but to be attuned to the solar cycle. The advent of artificial lighting changed everything, and the shift from incandescent to lower cost LED lighting further exacerbated the issues. In fact, in the last ten years, the amount and type of artificial light exposure humans experience has changed so dramatically that we can honestly say that, as a species, our whole relationship to light has been altered. Yet our biology hasn’t changed one bit in thousands of years. Hence this chapter.
COMMON QUESTIONS
How do I make this work if I’m stuck in the office all day

There is no need to be obsessive about this—it doesn’t have to interfere with your life. Still, by making some concerted effort toward viewing sunlight (or a 10,000 lux lamp) in the mornings, and sunlight in the late afternoons or early evenings, and avoiding bright light at night, you can dramatically improve your mood and energy levels, metabolism, and sleep—which of course bolsters all the rest. So try to get outdoors at these times if you can. Better yet, take a walk in the direction of the sun. Or even just make time to turn toward the sun and pause (and not look at your phone) for a few minutes in the parking lot before leaving work.
LIGHT PROTOCOL 3 Avoid Viewing Bright Light One Hour Before Your Bedtime
WHAT TO DO

• In the one hour before your bedtime, use only as much artificial light as necessary to safely carry out your nighttime activities. That recommendation holds until you wake up the next morning to begin your day.

• Be especially mindful to avoid viewing bright short wavelength light at this time. Avoid not just lights that appear blue, but also bright “white” LED lights, fluorescent lights, and screens, because they emit a lot of short wavelengths that stimulate cortisol release and inhibit melatonin.

• If you can’t avoid viewing bright short wavelength light, consider wearing short wavelength light blocking lenses. Not simply “blue blockers,” but these specific lenses. For anyone seeking an easier transition into sleep and better overall sleep, these glasses can be helpful.
HOW IT WORKS

In the first hour of your day, it takes a lot of bright light to stimulate cortisol release and activate the neural pathways in your brain and body that increase wakefulness. By comparison, in the final hour of your day, it takes very little bright light to wake you up. Moreover, melatonin, the hormone that promotes sleepiness, is potently inhibited by viewing bright light at any time of day or night. That’s why viewing bright light at night is a double whammy to your system: It makes you more alert and it makes you less sleepy by at least two different pathways.

The whole light-sensing and cortisol-releasing system is just not the same in the morning and at night. [^39] If you have ever felt that you are a vastly different person in the morning and at night, indeed you are. The key to using light as a tool to enhance your health is to understand this dynamic.
It all boils down to knowing when you woke up that morning and how many hours it has been since. Here’s a reference you can follow:
• A Day in the Light
• Phase 1: 0–1 hour after waking: You need to see a lot of bright light (Light Protocol 1).
• Phase 2: 6–10 hours after waking: Get some late afternoon or early evening sunlight in your eyes (Light Protocol 2).
• Phase 3: 10–14 hours after waking: Start dimming the lights, avoid bright light exposure to your eyes (this protocol).
• Phase 4: And finally, sleep…

Though by now you may be asking (or shouting), “What is all this ‘0–1 hour after waking, 6–10 hours after waking, and 1–2 hours before sleep’ stuff? No one lives this way! Why can’t you just give me a clock time?”

I’ve said this before, and I’ll say it again here: People follow different sleep-wake schedules, with some sleeping from 8:00 p.m. to 4:00 a.m. and others sleeping from 11:00 p.m. to 7:00 a.m. Still others work the night shift. Variation in people’s schedules makes it impossible for me to say, “Dim the lights and avoid viewing LED screens between 10:00 p.m. and 5:00 a.m.” or even “View bright light within an hour of sunrise.”

Also, the length of days varies according to location and time of year, and things like daylight further complicate matters. So I suggest you frame your sleep-wake schedule according to four phases. Once you try this approach to your days, and use light (or avoid it) accordingly, I’m certain it will improve your health and well-being.

It’s worth noting again that the clock times corresponding to the four phases will change if you were to, say, sleep in an extra hour or two, or wake up an hour earlier than is typical, or go to sleep an hour earlier or later. Not a problem! When it comes to the effects of light on cortisol and melatonin, we care about your biology, not an alarm. Start phase 1, for example, when you get up to begin your day. The light prescription for each phase does not change. This ought to bring a sense of control over your time—after all, no one wants to have to take care of their health strictly by the clock. Work, school, and other commitments have us doing that already.
In case any of this is confusing, here is how I use this system to structure my days (and nights).
My Phase 1 (as of writing)

I woke up at 7:00 a.m. I usually wake up at 5:45 or 6:00, but I was a bit more tired than usual from a long week of work and travel and I forgot to set my alarm. My sleep tracker told me that I fell asleep last night at about 10:15 p.m. At 7:00 a.m., I went for a walk outside for about twenty minutes, without a hat or sunglasses, and walked east in the direction of the sun. It was light out but overcast, with no hint even of the sun’s outline in the sky. But because it was fairly bright, I knew I was getting a decent amount of sunlight in my eyes, and therefore stimulating cortisol release. I was not at all concerned that I had somehow missed the window to use sunlight to boost my cortisol because my usual wake-up time is about 5:45. I know it’s about getting light in my eyes in the first hour after waking, not at a specific clock time, that matters.

I returned from my walk and, just to be sure that I spiked my morning cortisol sufficiently, I flipped on a 10,000 lux artificial light that I keep in my kitchen and kept it on while I went about my morning activities. Today was my day off from exercise (yesterday was leg day and generally the day after leg day is a day off from exercise for me; see Exercise Protocol 2).

From 8:00 a.m. until 11:00 a.m., I worked (podcast preparation, emails, and calls) at my desk with the overhead indoor lights on their brightest setting, and I sat near a window. I managed to get a few minutes outside during one of my work calls, and I paced while on the call, which allowed me to get a few extra steps in and a bit more sunlight. Around 11:00 a.m., I paused work to eat lunch, and then went back to work at my desk until about 2:00 p.m. On a less busy day, I might have taken my lunch outside.
My Phase 2

Given that I woke up at 7:00 a.m., this phase began six hours later at 1:00 p.m., and sure enough I started to feel a little sleepy around that time. I almost always experience a dip in energy about six hours after I wake up, even after a great night’s sleep. Some people don’t, but I do. I know it correlates, among other things, to the decline in cortisol that is normal, healthy, and expected at this time.

I know better than to push through this dip. I could take a prescription stimulant or slam an energy drink or two at that time, but why? I know there are other tools that won’t mess with my sleep. So from 2:00 to 2:30 I did a non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) session, which I described in chapters 1 and 3, and I emerged from it feeling refreshed. I drank some water and had a half cup of strong coffee and then dove back into work until about 5:00 p.m. (I can drink caffeine up until about 2:00 to 2:30 p.m. with no negative effect on my sleep, but for those more caffeine sensitive, take care.)
My Phase 3

Phase 3 is from ten hours until about fourteen hours after waking, so for today, that meant from 5:00 to 9:00 p.m. I used this time for more work. I also took a brief twenty-minute walk outside, then prepared and ate dinner. Then I started to wind down for the night. I dim the lights in my home to less than full blast starting in phase 3, and I recently started using the medium and long wavelength only setting in the evenings on lights that switch from full spectrum to medium and long wavelength emitting only. (See Sleep Protocol 3 for more on these bulbs.) They appear yellowish-orange rather than white. Several companies such as Bon Charge and Ra Optics now make LED bulbs that switch from full spectrum to medium and long wavelength emitting only (without having to program them for a specific time). You just flick the standard wall-mounted light switch. I love this simple technology because it’s so aligned with what our system needs, and it’s easy to use with no Wi-Fi or an app. And because they are LEDs, they last a very long time and are cost-efficient.
My Phase 4

This phase spans from the period starting fourteen hours after waking until the next morning when the new day starts. Today for me that meant from 9:00 p.m. on. For some time now, I have made it a practice to dim the lights in the final hours before I go to sleep. As I mentioned earlier in this chapter, people vary in their visual sensitivity to light. I am one of those who can be in front of a screen right up until I fall asleep. I have no trouble falling asleep, but it tends to make me wake up three to four hours later. When I started dimming the lights before bedtime, those mid-sleep awakenings all but stopped. I also switched to using long-wavelength-only light bulbs (red light) in the one to two hours before my bedtime. I still might wake up once in the middle of the night to use the bathroom but I have no trouble falling back asleep, and both my device-measured sleep scores and my subjective experience is that I am sleeping much better. If I’m out late or otherwise can’t use my typical indoor lighting in the hours before sleep—such as when I stay in a hotel—I wear ROKA Wind Down glasses that filter out short wavelength light. Often I wear them at home too, as I find they simplify this process.

Take note that phase 4 is where most people make seemingly small mistakes that cost them dearly in terms of health and well-being. There are two main reasons. With the advent of smartphones, and an endless stream of news, content, and the many other hooks that technology offers, it’s very easy to turn to a device. It’s also because most homes and hotels use LED lights nowadays, which emit short wavelengths that disrupt sleep. A bit later in the chapter, I’ll explain how to help with this. In the meantime, here are some ways to make phase 4 much easier and more effective:

• Keep it low and keep it dim. I suggest that any lighting you use in the final hours before you go to sleep come from desk lamps or floor lamps, that is, low light sources, and that, if possible, you avoid using overhead lights. The neurons in your eyes that signal to your brain that it is daytime are arranged across your neural retina (the light sensing tissue in the back of your eye) and they view the upper visual field, meaning the sky when you are outside and the ceiling when you are indoors. [^40] Many people find that using low, dim light sources in the one to two hours before bed makes it much easier to fall and stay asleep. [^41] This is pretty easy to do, and can make a big difference. You can go further still and use bulbs without short wavelengths, which thus appear yellow-orange, or even go with bulbs that emit purely long wavelengths, and thus appear red. Keep in mind this is not red light therapy. Red light therapy (explained later in this chapter) can be very beneficial for certain aspects of health but is altogether different from what we are discussing here. Medium-wavelength-only bulbs are relatively inexpensive and provide a nice yellow-amber glow. Admittedly, using long-wavelength-only bulbs will make your home look a little space age, but they are a great tool to help you sleep better. Either way, using dim, non-overhead lights without short wavelengths in the last one to two hours before bedtime reduces the activation of the retinal neurons that signal your brain to suppress melatonin and boost cortisol. [^42] As mentioned above, several companies have conveniently engineered bulbs that are full-spectrum-emitting (white) for the daytime, and with a simple flick of the light switch, become medium and long wavelength only emitting (yellow-amber or red). Incandescent versions of these exist too and are best, but they use more energy than LEDs, don’t last nearly as long, and are more costly. They are also a bit hard to find.

• Wear eyeglasses that filter out all short wavelength light. This approach is very convenient if you don’t want to change the lights in your home, or if you don’t have control over the lighting conditions in a certain environment, such as on planes, in hotels or airports, out with friends, et cetera. I designed the ROKA Wind Down glasses for use during the final hours before sleep, and I use them at home and when I travel. They differ from traditional blue blockers because they prevent all short wavelength light, not just blue light, from reaching your eyes. (Don’t wear them while driving because they make anything that is blue or green much harder to see or even invisible, and that could cause an accident.)

• Don’t worry about moonlight. You may be wondering if bright moonlight or even a roaring fire will stimulate the wakefulness pathways in your brain. The answer is, perhaps surprisingly, no. Although these are concentrated light sources, a bright full moon is less than 1 lux and while candles, fireplaces, and bonfires mostly emit medium and short wavelength light, it doesn’t radiate very far. If you have ever been camping and turned around from a roaring campfire, you’ve noticed that as soon as you are just a few paces away from it, you need a flashlight in order to see. We discussed the physics of this in chapter 1. So while fire and candles are great nighttime light sources from a cortisol-limiting and melatonin-preserving perspective, they are not very practical. Of course, if you’d like to read by candlelight or gather around a fire with friends, great. Just make sure the flames are extinguished when you’re finished. Be careful not to start a fire.

You may be wondering if all this attention to avoiding bright light in the hours before sleep is silly, neurotic biohacking. After all, you can find studies showing that blocking blue light improves people’s sleep to varying degrees, [^43] and you may be one of those people who can pass out with the TV or computer still at full brightness right in front of you. Indeed, there is considerable variation in the degree to which short wavelength light exposure alters people’s sleep. [^44] That said, having even just a dim 100 lux overhead light on while you sleep can alter the next-morning glucose levels. [^45] And that’s while sleeping, with eyes closed. The point is, altered sleep is not the only reason to avoid bright light in phase 4. Nighttime bright light exposure increases blood pressure [^46] and heart rate, and has been linked to weight gain and even a risk of obesity. [^47] Studies have found nighttime bright light to negatively impact next-day cognitive function [^48] and mood [^49] independent of bright light’s negative effects on sleep.

None of this is surprising to biologists who have studied the so-called non-image-forming visual system or the many opsins other than melanopsin that are present in our skin and other tissues for the last three decades. [^50] Myself included. We know, for instance, that the retinal neurons that respond to bright short wavelength light connect not only to your SCN but also to areas of your hypothalamus, such as the supraoptic nucleus, that are directly involved in sleep regulation. (I know, supraoptic sounds like suprachiasmatic but please don’t blame me, I didn’t name either one.) Your eyes also connect to your thalamus’s perihabenular nucleus, which has been nicknamed the anti-reward or disappointment center, [^51] given it actively inhibits dopamine release and is thought to increase feelings of depression when activated at night by, you guessed it, bright light.

The broader field of medicine is starting to incorporate these discoveries. Disrupting the light-dark cycle can affect lifespan. An international team of researchers conducted an enormous study in which 88,905 people enrolled in the UK Biobank, a database for collecting long-term health information, were given wearable light sensors for one week. [^52] The participants wore these wrist sensors for seven days, during which they went about their normal routine. The sensors recorded light exposure around the clock. At the end of the week, the researchers had data on 13 million hours of light exposure.

They grouped all the data according to daytime and night, categorizing participants according to light exposure during the day (between the hours of 7:30 a.m. and 8:30 p.m.) and light exposure during the night (between the hours of 12:30 a.m. and 6:00 a.m.). They then collected health data over a follow-up period of about eight years. For the 3,750 participants who died during the follow-up period, the researchers categorized mortality data according to cause of death.

They found that the brighter the night and the darker the day, the higher the risk of death; the link was dose dependent! The risk of death by any cause was up to 34 percent higher among those who got the most light exposure at night, compared to those with the least light exposure at night. The reverse was also true. The risk of death (by any cause) was up to 34 percent lower among the participants with the most light exposure during the day compared to those with the least. This connection held despite any other traits including age, sex, physical activity, smoking, drinking, and cardiovascular health.

There’s more. The analysis zoomed in on nighttime light exposure, grouping it into half hour increments and matching those increments with mortality data. The brightest lighting between 1:00 a.m. and 6:00 a.m. carried a risk of death by any cause that was 11 to 39 percent higher compared to the darkest lighting during this stretch of time. The risk of death due to cardiometabolic issues (heart attack, stroke, diabetes, nonalcoholic fatty liver disease) was 20 to 67 percent higher for the brightest lighting compared to the darkest lighting during this stretch of the night. The time frame here differs slightly from the one described in this protocol, but the exact times aren’t the point; the point is that viewing bright light at night is disruptive to your immediate and long-term health.

It’s true that this was a relatively brief study, using just a week’s worth of light exposure data. However, about three thousand participants repeated the study up to four times and the light exposure patterns were the same. Several other studies have found similar links. [^53] And the sheer volume of light exposure data in this one makes a persuasive case. As the researchers wrote in the 2024 publication of their study in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, “Across the general population, avoiding night light and seeking daylight may lead to reduction in disease burden, especially cardiometabolic diseases, and may increase longevity.”

In another large study, published in Nature Mental Health in 2023, researchers at the University of Manchester cross-referenced data on mental health with data on light, sleep, and physical activity from 86,722 individuals. [^54] Their analysis revealed a link between greater nighttime light exposure and higher risk for several mental health issues, including major depressive disorder, anxiety, post-traumatic stress disorder, and self-harm behavior. Greater daytime light exposure correlated with a reduced risk of these issues. They also found that people who experienced darker nights had fewer mental health symptoms, an effect that occurred independent of daytime light exposure. That is, bright-light-filled mornings and days and dark nights independently and additively promoted better mental health.

These large datasets deliver a clear and important message, one that typically goes unmentioned: Keeping the lights off during the late hours of your night is not just about getting great sleep; it is fundamentally important for your health and well-being.
LIGHT PROTOCOL 4 Expose Your Upper and Lower Body Skin to Sunlight During the Day
WHAT TO DO

• Get twenty to thirty minutes of outdoor sunlight exposure to your skin at least three times per week, and ideally every day. Wear the minimum amount of clothing that allows you to be comfortable and that is appropriate for your environment, without covering your entire body (for example, shirtless with shorts, or shorts and a tank top, or a swimsuit. In some cases, jeans and a short-sleeved T-shirt may be what’s called for). It is best that you do not wear a hat during this time. I discuss cold weather options below.
HOW IT WORKS

There is no substitute for sunlight. You could turn on every light in your home in the morning and daytime, make sure they are full-spectrum incandescent bulbs or wavelength-balanced full spectrum LEDs, view a 10,000 lux artificial light within an hour of waking up, and it still would not replace sunlight.

Each of those technologies can serve as a health-promoting supplement on days when you can’t get enough sunlight, and they can help boost the effects of sunlight, but they should not be used as an everyday replacement for sunlight. Think of them the same way you would supplements relative to nutritious food; they can help bridge deficiencies, and in some cases they can afford you a real mental or physical performance advantage. Yet no rational person would ever replace all their food with supplements on a consistent basis. Alas, because most people don’t understand how powerful light is as a tool for health, and that sunlight is a uniquely beneficial form of it, they engage with light in a way that is analogous to trying to live solely on supplements.

Actually, in many cases it’s even worse than that. People are spending the first hours of their day in sunless, dark, or dim indoor environments, viewing screens, and then continuing their days under artificial lights that seem bright but that are actually dim compared to sunlight. After sundown, they stay under those same lights, which are now far too bright for what is needed at night, and many view mostly short wavelength emitting screens. This is, in no uncertain terms, as bad as living on highly processed junk food. And it’s making a lot of people sick, mentally and physically.

Getting sunlight on our skin is as much a cornerstone of health as sleep, exercise, or nutrition. It’s hard for most people to fully grasp this, especially given that we all have heard how damaging UV light is for our skin. Yet, we need to embrace what is special and beneficial about sunlight and incorporate it into our daily lives. And no, you do not have to live in California, or run around shirtless or in a bathing suit outside. You simply need to know how the energy present in sunlight impacts every cell in your body: your brain, hair, skin, liver, heart, your hormones, neurotransmitters, immune system, and on and on.
And so, on to the science.

Sunlight is the absolute best source of long wavelength light, from the red end of the visible spectrum into non-visible near-infrared and IR wavelengths. It is difficult to overstate how important these longer wavelengths are for our health, in particular for our mitochondria, the energy producing organelles within our cells. (I’ll cover the uses of LWL devices that purely emit red, NIR, and IR light in the next protocol.)

Sunlight contains short wavelength UV light, which as we discussed earlier in this chapter, triggers the production of vitamin D in the skin. Although this vitamin (which also acts as a hormone) is available in some foods, supplements can replace sunlight as a stimulus for vitamin D, [^55] yet our bodies evolved to use sun-induced vitamin D in multiple ways that supplements may not mimic.

For example, vitamin D is important for hormone health and the reproductive system. A multi-institution study on mice and humans looked at the effects specifically of UVB (the ultraviolet wavelength that penetrates the skin) on reproductive-related hormones and behavior. [^56] They found that mice exposed to UVB light for one hour per day showed enhanced mating behavior and physiology—greater attraction for one another, larger ovaries, and more testosterone—in both the male and female mice. Moreover, male mice showed a greater attraction to UVB-treated female mice, likely due to how elevated testosterone and estrogen levels in females impacted their appearance and scent, making them more attractive. More interestingly, the researchers saw similar patterns in people. According to their findings, published in Cell Reports in 2021, participants reported increased romantic interest in others following time in the sun. The data also showed heightened testosterone levels linked to this exposure in both men and women. Testosterone and estrogen levels—both of which impact romantic desire and feelings of well-being in men and women—were highest in the longer days of spring and summer relative to shorter winter and fall days.

This effect appears to relate to a molecule called p53 expressed in a type of skin cell called keratinocytes. Mice in which p53 had been removed did not exhibit the same changes following UVB exposure. This detail emphasizes the importance of having sunlight reach not only our eyes, but also our skin.

Here’s another: UV light from sunlight also reduces physical pain. In 2017, a group of researchers reported a study in which they exposed mice to UVB (midrange ultraviolet light, abundant in sunlight) radiation and then tested various parameters relating to the HPA axis. [^57] This brain pathway is the core mechanism behind our stress response (as discussed in chapters 1 and 3). [^58] They found a link between UVB radiation and the stimulation of corticotropin-releasing hormone, which helps us cope with social stress, [^59] and endogenous beta endorphins, a type of opioid our body naturally produces in response to psychological distress. [^60] Although this work focused on mice, the results point toward a potentially crucial and unappreciated role for sunlight, in particular UV light—which most people generally think of as the aspect of sunlight to be avoided.

Excessive UV light exposure will cause sunburn and increase your risk for certain forms of skin cancer. So, while UV light from the sun has many benefits, it is still important to avoid too much exposure and sunburn.
A Word About Sunscreen

Of course, no one wants a sunburn. One’s risk of sunburn and skin cancer varies depending on factors such as skin tone and inherited susceptibility to skin cancer. All dermatologists agree that any amount of sunburn is bad for us, so bear that in mind. And all agree that excessive exposure to sunlight leads to more rapid aging of the skin too. Excessive skin exposure to UV light, in particular, mutates our skin cell DNA and destroys keratinocytes, which give skin its suppleness. So the takeaway message is to avoid sunburn at all costs.

I don’t burn easily but if I am going to be outside at a time of day when the UV index is high, I either rely on a physical barrier—hat and long sleeves—or I apply a mineral-based sunscreen that uses zinc oxide (not nano zinc) as the only active ingredient. People debate whether chemical-based sunscreens are bad for hormone health and my read of the literature is yes, they can be; but that debate aside, no one argues whether physical barriers or mineral-based-only sunscreen are useful and safe. It’s therefore an obvious choice in my opinion, especially since purely mineral-based sunscreens now come in forms that don’t leave a white paste on your skin, are reef- and ocean life–safe, and aren’t too expensive. I use Le Rub, which is an all-day mineral-based sunscreen that comes in a metal tube. Why is that relevant? Well, I am among a growing number of people who don’t want more microplastics in my body if I can help it. After hosting Shanna Swan, PhD, professor of environmental medicine and public health at Mount Sinai School of Medicine, on my podcast, I did an audit of easy-to-eliminate endocrine disruptors, and I decided to find a non-plastic container, non-endocrine-disrupting sunscreen. Le Rub meets those criteria, smells great, and applies clear, unlike many zinc oxide sunscreens that remain as a white paste on the skin. I liked it so much that I became a partial owner of the company—so I am now very biased, but for the very reason that it’s the only sunscreen I’ll use.

Definitely check the UV index before spending a lot of time in the sun. A simple web search of “What is the UV index at different times today in [enter city and country]?” will yield you a result in less than ten seconds. It will tell you when to be careful about excess UV exposure.

But don’t avoid the sun entirely! Getting sun exposure on your skin not only supports various hormone production pathways as described here, it may also help you live longer. A Swedish study looking at mortality rates among 29,518 women found that greater sun exposure correlated with lower all-cause risk of death. [^61] In fact, people who spent the least amount of time in the sun had nearly double the mortality risk during the twenty years of the study compared to those who spent the most time in the sun. Obviously, there are likely to be many factors at play here: More time outside usually means more fresh air, movement, social interaction, et cetera, not just sunlight. Yet the data correlating different amounts of sunlight exposure to health and longevity all seem to point in the same direction: Getting sunlight on your skin is beneficial. Interestingly, that work followed an earlier study of nearly forty thousand women that found a reduction in mortality linked to exposure to ultraviolet light coming directly from the sun, and yet an increase in mortality linked to ultraviolet light from artificial sources. [^62]

Why would UV light from sunlight help and yet the (seemingly) same UV light from artificial sources harm us? One idea is that because sunlight has a balance of short, medium, and long wavelengths—each at particular energies and with their own unique health-promoting effects—they synergize. UV without adequate longer wavelengths—such as what comes from most LEDs—is thought to be detrimental to our cells. [^63]

I’ll dive more into the ways that different wavelengths of light impact our cells in the next protocol, but for now here are some crucial things to know: No single wavelength of light is “bad” or “good.” Longer wavelengths of light are absorbed by the water in our mitochondria and help “charge” the mitochondria like batteries, making them more efficient at producing ATP [^64] and possibly even helping cells to make more mitochondria. Longer wavelength light also helps offset the negative effects of reactive oxygen species (ROS)—a normal by-product of cellular function that, if in excess, damages our cells. [^65] ROS are thought to be a major factor in the reduced energy levels and organ dysfunction we experience with aging. [^66] Long wavelength light can pass through our skin, eyelids, our ribs, and even our skull to reach our brain and other internal organs, and so helps to promote their health, largely by improving mitochondrial function as described above. [^67] How wild is that?! Sunlight also contains abundant amounts of medium wavelength light—yellows and oranges, or in technical terms about 500 to 620 nanometer light, which has been shown to reduce headache pain, stimulate blood flow, and reduce inflammation. [^68]

Artificial lights of course contain some of these wavelengths but not in the same balance as is present in sunlight. Incandescent bulbs are better than LEDs in this respect, but nowadays LEDs and fluorescent lights are almost exclusively used for indoor lighting because they cost less, use less energy, and last longer. Most LEDs are enriched with short wavelengths which, unless balanced out by long wavelength light, have been shown to increase ROS and damage mitochondria. [^69] Some LEDs and fluorescent lights even emit small amounts of UV. [^70] This all becomes a problem for cellular health when we are under these lights all day and not getting the protective effects of long wavelength light or enough sunlight. It’s rather incredible that while so many people are afraid of UV from sunlight, they may be unaware how the many hours of daily (and nightly) exposure to short wavelength light can damage our health. The remedy: balanced wavelength exposure from sunlight, done safely of course. The protocols in this chapter represent the key times and ways to do just that. The other remedy: incandescent rather than LED indoor lighting, and limiting your short wavelength light exposure after nightfall.

Still not convinced that light is medicine? I mentioned above how researchers found that UV light from sunlight reduces physical pain, and there are studies of humans experiencing similar effects. In a study of eighty-nine patients who’d undergone spinal surgery, those who stayed on the bright side of the hospital, and were therefore exposed to 46 percent more intense sunlight than those staying on the dim side of the hospital, reported less pain-related stress and a bit less pain, and required 22 percent less pain medication. [^71] Similar results have been reported in the relief of fibromyalgia among women [^72] and in a small study of US military veterans, chronic lower back pain. [^73] Preliminary research indicates that the underlying mechanism here brings us back to the intrinsically photosensitive retinal ganglion cells, which don’t just connect to the SCN but also communicate light information (through a relay station) to the periaqueductal gray area, a region that is crucial to pain modulation. [^74]

And, as discussed in other protocols in this chapter, regular, consistent light exposure also enhances mood. [^75] Data suggest that individuals exposed to moderate amounts of UVB—which is abundant in sunlight—may have a lower risk for depression. [^76] A review of seven different studies evaluating the link between ultraviolet radiation and mood concluded that the evidence supports this beneficial connection. [^77]

The simple takeaway here is this: Get some sunlight on your skin for at least thirty minutes per day, as many days per week as possible. How much skin you can directly expose will of course vary by weather, location, and circumstances, but do it. Check the UV index and learn what you need without getting a sunburn. Don’t get a sunburn. And while sunlight through a window is not the same as going outside, if you can make your indoor environment brighter from sunlight, do it. Otherwise, think seriously about how much conventional LED light exposure you’re getting and, if it’s a lot, consider switching to full spectrum LED lights. And given the direct and protective benefits of long wavelength light, consider the next protocol.

What if I live in a dark, gloomy place or it’s a dark, gloomy time of year, as it is in much of the UK, Scandinavia, or the Pacific Northwest, especially during the winter
