LIGHT PROTOCOL 5 Expose Your Skin and Eyes to Long Wavelength Light (Red, Near-IR, and Infrared)
WHAT TO DO

• Use a long-wavelength-light-emitting (LWL) device for ten to thirty minutes, three to seven days per week. For general health effects (energy, skin appearance, exercise recovery, etc.), the goal is to illuminate the largest area of your skin, face, and head that you can. This will obviously depend on what LWL device you have access to and the amount of time you can devote to this.
HOW IT WORKS

Red light therapy has become a popular health trend. Red light saunas, red light panels, red light beds, masks, even red-light helmets to promote hair growth… the list goes on. Despite their space age look, this is a trend with genuine scientific support behind it. Several leading dermatology journals including JAMA Dermatology have published in-depth reviews on the use of red light to treat different skin conditions, [^78] and other fields of medicine including ophthalmology are following suit by exploring how red light can be used to offset, or even reverse, age-related decline in organ function. Most of these devices also emit near-infrared (NIR) and/or infrared (IR) light as well. For simplicity and accuracy, I will refer to all such devices collectively as LWL devices. Of course, the exact wavelengths and intensities of light that different LWL devices emit vary. Some also emit short wavelength light. I’ll touch on some of the different features to look for when considering use of different photobiomodulation devices at the end of this protocol.

First, let’s discuss what photobiomodulation is really about. In the context of light, photobiomodulation involves exposing a portion (or all) of your skin to a specific range of wavelengths, typically long wavelength light, for ten, twenty, or thirty minutes, three to seven days per week. As I mentioned above, for general health effects the goal is to illuminate the largest area of your skin, face, and head that you can. Smaller handheld LWL devices that illuminate a limited area can be helpful for pain reduction and to promote wound healing in specific areas, [^79] but the most impressive effects of long wavelength light photobiomodulation are generally achieved with whole-body long-wavelength light exposure using a large LWL panel, or a red light bed or LWL blanket, and by illuminating both sides of your body, either simultaneously or sequentially.

Long wavelength light can penetrate the skin’s surface and once inside your body, it can scatter up to 8 centimeters. [^80] Longer wavelengths in the infrared range have been shown to even pass through thin clothing such as T-shirts and through your torso. [^81] That might sound scary but remember that long wavelength light is low energy non-ionizing radiation, so it is safe, and all evidence points to long wavelength light having a protective and a health-promoting effect on your cells. Put simply, exposing your skin to long wavelength light in this way is a good thing. The main reason? It promotes mitochondrial health.

Mitochondrial health is a term used often these days, so before going any further, let’s further define what this means. As discussed several times already in this book, cellular energy is generated in the form of a chemical called adenosine triphosphate, or ATP. Mitochondria are crucial for ATP production, as well as for making our hormones and neurotransmitters. Mitochondria contain an enzyme called cytochrome c oxidase, and it can absorb light. [^82] In that way, cytochrome c oxidase is similar to the photopigments in your eye that absorb specific wavelengths of light, and that kick off the cascade of events in your eyes and brain that lead to sight. The difference is that cytochrome c oxidase is inside the cells of your body and brain, and its job is to support the formation of ATP for your cells to use. The way it does that is by moving electrons from one protein to the next inside the mitochondria. (Briefly: Like any compound, proteins are made of molecules; molecules are made of atoms bonded together; atoms are made of subatomic particles including protons, which are positively charged, electrons, which are negatively charged, and neutrons, which carry no charge.) That process releases energy that moves protons, also in the mitochondria, and because protons carry an electrical charge, it sort of works like a battery.

The business of moving protons in mitochondria isn’t just about making energy; it takes energy too. The first law of thermodynamics is that energy can’t be created or destroyed, it can only be transformed. Long wavelength light energy from the sun that is absorbed by cytochrome c oxidase is transformed by your mitochondria to help create ATP. So, in a loose sense, we are solar powered.

The absorption of long wavelength light by cytochrome c oxidase also causes nitric oxide—a chemical that can impair mitochondrial function—to dislodge from the organelle, which then allows cytochrome c oxidase to use oxygen more efficiently. That enhances something called mitochondrial respiration, a process critical for converting nutrients in our blood into ATP. [^83] Bam! Long wavelength light can enhance cellular ATP production through at least two proposed mechanisms.

Long wavelength light also may support mitochondrial energy production through a third mechanism involving the increased action of intracellular melatonin, which can help prevent oxidative damage. [^84] Until now we have discussed melatonin only as a hormone produced by the pineal gland that promotes sleepiness. However, many cells throughout our body produce melatonin. Long wavelength light may allow intracellular melatonin to act more effectively as an antioxidant, helping to repair some of the oxidative damage that is a normal consequence of cellular metabolism. One potential benefit of this pathway is that it may reduce some of the harm caused by excessive UV light exposure. [^85] As we discuss next, the implications of that are, literally, visible.
How It Affects Your Skin

Long wavelength light can promote the youthful look of skin, reduce acne, and accelerate wound healing. [^86] Studies have also investigated long wavelength light as a tool to treat wrinkles, scars, burns, and other causes of discoloration of the skin.

In one study of ninety-three patients, administration of rapid pulses of 590-nanometer light was linked to reduced signs of aging. [^87] In another study by the same research group, ninety patients were given pulses of 590-nanometer light in eight treatments over four weeks. [^88] The investigators took digital images of the patients at the start of the study and over the following twelve months and found reduced signs of aging in the vast majority of participants. They also evaluated tissue samples from ten of the patients and found increased collagen, a protein that provides structure and elasticity to skin, in all the subjects who received this therapy. The wavelength measuring 590 nanometers is in the orange-red range of the visible spectrum and, as noted above, longer wavelengths (600–850 nm) can pass even deeper into the skin layers. Indeed, investigations found even more impressive reductions in wrinkles following treatment with 633-nanometer (red) light combined with 830-nanometer light, which falls in the near-infrared range. [^89]

There also are benefits to combining long wavelength light with short wavelength light, at least for improving skin. Dermatologists at Mount Sinai Medical Center, in New York, treated twenty-two people with mild to moderate acne with eight sessions of light therapy that used alternating exposure to blue (short wavelength) and red (long wavelength) light, for twenty minutes per exposure. [^90] Four weeks after the treatment ended, participants showed a 46 percent reduction in acne lesions. At eight weeks post-treatment, the reduction had reached 81 percent. A study from Imperial College of Science, Technology, and Medicine, in London, with 107 patients, reported similar outcomes. [^91] That is pretty remarkable if you ask me.
How It Affects Your Metabolism

There’s another impressive effect of long wavelength light therapy. Exposing your skin to long wavelength light can reduce your glucose levels, and increase your metabolism. It seems unlikely, but it turns out to be true. All we have to do is look at the data. In a recent study, researchers shined a 670-nanometer light on subjects’ backs for fifteen minutes and measured their glucose levels in response to ingestion of a sugary drink—a classic research method to measure blood sugar regulation. [^92] They observed a 27.7 percent reduction in glucose in comparison to control subjects that did not receive the light exposure. Measurements of oxygen uptake confirmed that their metabolism had risen significantly, which makes sense given that long wavelength light exposure can increase ATP production by as much as 100 to 200 percent.

I heard some people interpreting this study as meaning that eating under short-wavelength-only light sources like conventional LED lights lowers your metabolism, even going so far as to argue that obesity is on the rise because of short wavelength light overuse. While that might be the case, that is not what this study shows. It is reasonable, however, to conclude on the basis of this study that eating outside in the sunlight or even in the shade on a sunny day where long wavelength light is abundant, or eating near a LWL device, may be beneficial for those seeking to improve their blood sugar regulation. Getting exercise and proper nutrition per the recommendations in chapters 2 and 4 are the major factors for healthy blood sugar regulation. Nevertheless, long wavelength light can certainly be used to augment proper exercise and nutrition, and it may be a particularly useful tool for regulating blood sugar and metabolism when exercise is restricted due to injury, weather, travel, and the like.
How It Affects Your Eyesight

The effects go on. Long wavelength light has been helpful in preserving eye health too. First, a little bit about your eyes: The photoreceptor cells in your eyes consume more energy than any other cell in your brain or body. [^93] Think about that for a second: more than any other cell, meaning more than all the rest of your brain cells, your liver, even your muscle cells… and that is true even if you were to run a marathon and use those muscle cells, every single day! Your photoreceptors are almost always active, even in the dark. The point is your photoreceptors produce and use a ton of energy around the clock. The energy they draw on comes in the form of ATP, and ATP production, as you now know, depends on mitochondria. Not surprisingly, your photoreceptors are packed with mitochondria [^94] and they produce a ton of ATP, but with all that ATP production comes a high amount of free radicals, and as I mentioned earlier in this protocol, those impose stress on the cells, which over time damages the mitochondria. Exposure of the eyes to long wavelength light—the red, near-infrared, and infrared end of the spectrum—both reduces the presence of free radicals [^95] and helps stimulate the production of ATP by the mechanisms discussed above. So it makes sense that long wavelength light therapy might have a role in preserving or improving our photoreceptors… and therefore, our vision.

And indeed, that’s what the data show. Work by neuroscientist Glen Jeffery (mentioned at the start of this chapter) investigated whether direct viewing of long wavelength light could improve people’s vision. In one study, he and his team enrolled twenty-four people between the ages of twenty-eight and seventy-two to look at a 670-nanometer beam (red light) from a flashlight for three minutes per day for two weeks. [^96] Participants under the age of forty showed no change in vision. But those around forty years and older showed a greater ability to discern colors at the end of the experiment. In a second study, the investigators used the same intervention but at a less intense level, meaning the light was not as close to the participants’ eyes (though it was still 670 nanometers, or red light) and found that to be sufficient to boost vision for one week, again among those about forty years old and over. [^97] The improvement in vision in these studies reached 20 percent among some participants, which is a significant and compelling result. The researchers also observed a reduction in drusen, which are fat deposits that accumulate in the eyes as we age [^98] and that are connected to age-related macular degeneration.

Importantly, the second study by Jeffery and colleagues found that the timing of the long wavelength light therapy mattered. The benefit to vision occurred only if the red light was seen in the morning, likely because mitochondrial function changes across the twenty-four-hour cycle, with a particular sensitivity to light then. It is worth noting that the range of benefit was wide; some individuals experienced a greater boost than others. The underlying reasons of who benefits and who doesn’t are not yet clear. Studies ongoing in Glen Jeffery’s lab are now focused on the use of long wavelength light therapy for advanced macular degeneration, retinitis pigmentosa, and glaucoma.

To be clear: The most common causes of vision loss—cataracts, glaucoma, macular degeneration, and diabetes [^99]—are unlikely to be caused by lack of long wavelength light exposure, although that possibility hasn’t been ruled out either. All these forms of vision loss are typically associated with aging, and some forms have a clear genetic contribution as well. Everyone should get an annual eye exam and get their eye pressures checked for glaucoma once a year. Do not rely on this protocol as the only way to treat or prevent these conditions. That said, the ability for long wavelength light to slow, halt, or reverse vision loss is gaining more and more support.

Along those lines, you might be wondering how exactly to adopt this protocol. Turns out it’s very easy: Expose your face to long wavelength light from a concentrated red light source (not laser!) for five to ten minutes once or twice per week, and do it within three hours of waking. You don’t need to put the light source terribly close to your eyes either; it’s best you do it at a distance that is comfortable and doesn’t force you to close your eyes. However, in this and other long wavelength light protocols, you are welcome to close your eyes. It won’t hinder the effect unless you wear dark occluding glasses—the ones that make it look like you’re going into a tanning bed (which is UV by the way; I do not recommend those for reasons that ought to be obvious by now). Long wavelength light easily passes through your eyelids to reach your photoreceptors. You can get enough retinal long wavelength light exposure as a consequence of whole body long wavelength light illumination too. There is no evidence that more frequent or longer exposures than five to ten minutes once or twice per week are needed for the visual system benefits, but also no evidence that more would be harmful. Remember, the effects were only observed in people forty and older and only if it was done within one to three hours of waking.
SOURCES TO CONSIDER
You have a lot of options when it comes to long wavelength light sources for photobiomodulation—for this use, and others. I will discuss these in order from the least to the most costly.
Option 1: The sun.

The sun is rich with long wavelength light and it’s zero cost, but you get less long wavelength light exposure on overcast days and for most, it’s not practical to expose your whole body to it for ten to thirty minutes, three to seven days per week. And while UV light is less of an issue when the sun is low in the sky around sunrise and sunset, for people who miss those windows of opportunity, you will need to take measures to avoid getting excessive UV exposure. As mentioned above, check the UV index for your location. Of course, never, ever, force yourself to stare at the sun. Blink as needed to protect your eyes. The reflex to do so is the guide to follow. Or close your eyes; remember, long wavelength light radiation will reach your eyes just fine through your eyelids as long as you’re not wearing sunglasses. It’s fine to wear corrective lens eyeglasses or contacts for the reasons discussed in chapter 1.
Option 2: A LWL device.

There are tons of options out there on the market now, and they vary a lot by cost. It’s a bit overwhelming. You’ll often see claims from companies that their LWL device is best because it has “more power” than others on the market, but that’s a bit misleading. Differences in the intensity of devices are negligible when you consider that just getting closer to a device and/or extending the duration that you use it can compensate for most differences in intensity. Which you decide to use will likely be dictated by your budget and access. Small handheld units the size of a sandwich can cost $500, some full body panels $10,000 to $12,000, and the LWL “red light beds” and capsules can cost from $25,000 to more than $100,000. (Sunshine when the UV is low may be sounding pretty good right now.)

Some people like LWL face masks or helmets for skin or hair, respectively. A review of the research on a phototherapy mask, published in the Journal of Clinical and Aesthetic Dermatology in 2018, concluded that this light therapy device was effective for treating acne and psoriasis, healing wounds, and reducing actinic keratosis, rough and scaly skin that can result from years of sun exposure. [^100] This study was not funded by the device manufacturer, but it was authored by the head of a private dermatology research institute rather than an academic laboratory research group. That said, there is no reason to think the results with a mask would be any different from the results with a light panel, except that the light is hitting a smaller area of skin. I think the panels are the most versatile as you can expose whatever body areas you want but obviously cost compare and decide for yourself.

After deciding what is affordable for you, the most important factor in selecting a LWL device is that it exclusively emits long wavelength light of about 600 nm or longer. (We don’t see infrared light, which is why these are often called red light devices.) Generally speaking, the broader the range of long wavelengths that a device emits, the better the results. In other words, the most effective devices emit red, near-IR, and IR (600–850+ nm) light. The Jeffery lab studies used red light at wavelengths of about 600 to 670 nanometers to produce the visual system benefits, while light at wavelengths of 850 nanometers and above penetrated into and through the body—which again, is a good thing. As another rule, LWL devices that feel warm to the skin at the distance you use them are going to be more effective, because that encourages more blood flow and lymphatic flow, and in doing so helps improve the anti-inflammation effects of long wavelength light. Some LWL devices also include non-UV short wavelength light, which can be helpful for pain relief.

Most LWL devices use LEDs, but a few use incandescent bulbs. Lasers, which deliver a focused ray of light, tend to be higher in intensity—and they are brighter. I don’t recommend these for home use. Low-level laser therapy (LLLT) is a medical intervention and anyone using it to address aging or skin issues that are often treated with topical creams or other prescription interventions, such as wounds, acne, or other chronic skin conditions, should consult with a physician to ensure this approach is safe for you.

As mentioned above, I strive to take brief walks outside throughout the day just before or after meals, and pace outside when on work calls, if I can. Obviously I wear clothing during these times, but even with most skin covered, I’m sure to get some long wavelength light exposure, especially on clear days. I also use a JOOVV LWL panel for ten to thirty minutes once a day, generally three to five days per week. The JOOVV panels are medical grade and emit red and IR light; note they are a Huberman Lab podcast sponsor. I also really like the LWL incandescent bulbs from SaunaSpace as they generate heat, and emit 600 to 1,000 nanometer light. They make actual red light saunas too using those same bulbs; they look like a small canvas tent with a large-bulb long wavelength light–incandescent panel inside, and they are terrific because they too generate a lot of heat—which is what you want for a sauna session—and have all the features of long wavelength light photobiomodulation.

I confess I am not a fan of most other long wavelength light, or red light, saunas that use LEDs because they generally don’t get hot enough to trigger the benefits of dry or wet traditional saunas. [^101] Dry heat saunas can have great benefits for cardiovascular health, for growth hormone production, and for enhancing red blood cell production leading to endurance performance enhancement, but those effects are generally seen using temperatures ranging from roughly 180 to 210 degrees Fahrenheit. Most red light saunas just don’t get hot enough to create those benefits. Rather than view any one LWL device as “the best,” consider what you are able to access and afford, and use that. And remember the best and least expensive long wavelength light emitting source: good ol’ sunlight.
